claims.text: The initial material is a conventional single-phase refractory HEA, typically with a BCC structure.
Controlled HPHT treatment followed by aging can induce stepwise coherent nanoprecipitation in a single-phase refractory HEA.
The treatment will produce a uniform dispersion of coherent nanoprecipitates.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces relieve stress concentrations associated with premature crack initiation.
The nanoprecipitates impede dislocation motion and thereby increase strength.
The nanoprecipitates increase stiffness and Young's modulus by impeding dislocation motion.
Coherent interfaces promote homogeneous plastic deformation and improved ductility by avoiding stress localization.
The balance between precipitate strengthening and matrix toughness is controlled by nanoprecipitate size, spacing, and coherency.
The treatment will improve yield strength by approximately 30–50% relative to an untreated baseline.
The treatment will improve fracture strength by approximately 30–50% relative to an untreated baseline.
The treatment will increase elongation by approximately 10–20% relative to an untreated baseline.
The treatment will maintain or slightly enhance Young's modulus.
Excessively high temperature or prolonged holding will produce incoherent or overly coarse precipitates that negate the mechanical benefits.
Insufficient diffusion during overly rapid processing will prevent the beneficial coherent precipitate structure from forming.
The benefits diminish at temperature extremes where the nanoprecipitates become unstable.
Excessive nanoprecipitate density may cause brittleness.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis promises an improvement in Young's modulus, whereas the predicted outcome allows the modulus merely to remain stable.
A stable or only slightly enhanced Young's modulus is presented as an expected successful outcome, but an improvement below 10% is also given as a falsifying result.
